blocks.text: 1. Hallucinations

blocks.alt: An LLM can produce a confident false answer

blocks.text: Limitations of LLMs closed by pointing here. This topic examines one of the most consequential weaknesses of generative models: the specific failure mode previewed earlier.
Hallucination means confident, fluent text that is factually wrong or entirely made up.
2. Recapping The Preview
Hallucinations was previewed in that earlier topic as the specific failure mode covered here in full depth.
This topic works through the details only briefly gestured at before.
3. Recapping The Hallucination Preview
That earlier preview, in Why RAG Is Needed, described hallucination as filling gaps with confident, invented text.
This topic examines exactly why that happens and what can be done about it.
4. Why Generation Can Produce Confident Falsehoods

blocks.alt: An LLM predicts the most likely next token, not necessarily true

blocks.text: A model, relying on next token prediction, picks each next word based on learned probability, not verified fact.
Fluent, grammatically confident text can still be entirely, factually wrong, which is the core mechanism behind hallucination.
5. Hallucination Types

blocks.alt: Factual error, fabricated source, and logical inconsistency are hallucination types

blocks.text: Factual hallucinations invent specific, checkable details like dates, names, or numbers.
Faithfulness hallucinations, by contrast, misrepresent or contradict real, provided source text, an important distinction to keep straight.

blocks.text: 6. Recapping Temperature And Hallucination
Higher temperature settings, covered under Temperature, increase the chance of surprising, invented output.
Lower temperature reduces that risk, but never eliminates it completely.
7. Grounding As The Core Mitigation

blocks.alt: Ungrounded generation is compared against generation grounded in retrieved text

blocks.text: Grounding generation in retrieved text, the core idea behind Retrieval-Augmented Generation, is the most direct way to reduce hallucination.
It gives the model real facts to draw from, instead of relying purely on memorized patterns, which is the core mitigation for hallucination.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Grounding generation in retrieved text, as used in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, is the single most effective, practical technique for reducing hallucination in real systems.

blocks.text: 8. Hallucinations Still Occur With RAG

blocks.alt: RAG reduces but does not eliminate hallucination

blocks.text: Even with real, retrieved passages, a model can still misread or misrepresent them.
RAG reduces hallucination considerably, but does not eliminate it entirely.

blocks.text: 9. Detecting And Measuring Hallucination

blocks.alt: A generated answer is compared against the retrieved source

blocks.text: Faithfulness, covered as a later topic in this course, measures how well an answer matches its retrieved source.
This gives teams a concrete, measurable way to track hallucination over time.
10. Recognizing Why Hallucination Matters So Much For RAG System Design

blocks.alt: A high-stakes domain points toward prioritizing strong grounding

blocks.text: RAG reduces hallucination through real, retrieved grounding.
Careful evaluation remains necessary even with retrieval in place, since hallucination is reduced, not eliminated.
11. Worked Example
The example below compares an ungrounded guess against a grounded, retrieved answer.

code.content:
retrieved_passage = "The company was founded in 2015 by three engineers in Austin, Texas."

def ungrounded_answer(query):
    # a plain model without retrieval, guessing based on learned patterns alone
    return "The company was founded in 2012 by a single entrepreneur in San Francisco."

def grounded_answer(query, passage):
    # grounding the answer in the retrieved passage
    if "founded" in query.lower() and "2015" in passage:
        return "Based on retrieved context: the company was founded in 2015 by three engineers in Austin, Texas."
    return "No relevant information found in the retrieved passage."

query = "When and where was the company founded?"
print(f"Query: {query}")
print(f"Ungrounded answer: {ungrounded_answer(query)}")
print(f"Grounded answer: {grounded_answer(query, retrieved_passage)}")

print("\nNotice: the ungrounded answer is confident but entirely wrong,")
print("while the grounded answer matches the real, retrieved source")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the ungrounded answer confidently inventing incorrect details, while the grounded answer correctly matches the real retrieved passage.

blocks.text: 12. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a fluent, confident answer is automatically a factually correct one.
Treating RAG as a complete guarantee against hallucination rather than a strong reduction.
Ignoring faithfulness hallucinations, where the model misreads its own real, provided source.
Skipping any measurement of hallucination, treating it as unmeasurable rather than trackable.

blocks.text: 13. Key Takeaways

items: Hallucination means confident, fluent text that is factually wrong or entirely made up.
A model picks each next word based on learned probability, not verified fact.
Factual hallucinations invent details; faithfulness hallucinations misrepresent real source text.
Higher temperature increases hallucination risk; lower temperature reduces but never eliminates it.
Grounding generation in real, retrieved passages is the single most effective practical mitigation.
Even with retrieved passages, a model can still misread or misrepresent them.
RAG reduces hallucination considerably, but does not eliminate it entirely.
Faithfulness metrics give teams a concrete, measurable way to track hallucination over time.
